metadata.title: Survey of Adult Skills 2023 – Country Notes: Italy

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The Survey of Adult Skills is administered as a household survey with a personal interview and a self-completed assessment delivered on tablets. In Italy, the analytic results are based on a sample drawn to be representative of the adult population aged 16–65 (about 37.4 million residents), and the report notes that analyses were conducted to check that non-response does not introduce significant bias. The country notes do not specify the exact survey weight variable names or whether replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) were used, so the precise weighting implementation cannot be extracted from the provided text. For interpreting the reported means and proficiency-level shares, readers should treat the estimates as survey-weighted and uncertainty intervals (95% confidence intervals) as reflecting the complex design, even though the specific weight variables are not documented in this excerpt.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This country note reports descriptive proficiency results (means on 500-point scales and shares at proficiency levels) and related associations with outcomes, rather than training or evaluating an ML model on PV-based cognitive achievement. While the Survey of Adult Skills uses proficiency estimation based on task success, the excerpt does not document a PV-combining or PV-imputation strategy, and the reported outputs are presented as OECD proficiency estimates and level distributions. Missing-data handling is therefore not reported in the provided text, and the absence should be treated as a reporting gap for methodological transparency rather than evidence that no missingness occurred.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the Italy 2022–23 Survey of Adult Skills sample of adults aged 16–65 (n=4,847) drawn to be representative of the resident adult population. The report indicates that doorstep questionnaire respondents are generally excluded when comparing across cycles to maximise comparability, and it also notes that some analyses exclude doorstep-only respondents due to language barriers. Beyond these comparability exclusions, the excerpt does not specify additional item-level or case-level exclusions for the analytic sample used for the reported proficiency and outcome tables.

data.outcome_summary: The OECD Survey of Adult Skills 2023 country note for Italy reports adults’ proficiency in three domains—literacy, numeracy, and adaptive problem solving—based on tablet-administered tasks completed by adults aged 16–65 in 2022–23. Italy’s mean proficiency is below the OECD average in all three domains (literacy 245, numeracy 244, adaptive problem solving 231 on 500-point scales), with large shares at low proficiency (e.g., 35% at Level 1 or below in literacy and numeracy; 46% at or below Level 1 in adaptive problem solving). The note also documents subgroup differences by age (older adults 55–65 lower than 25–34), education attainment (tertiary education higher than upper secondary and below), and immigrant background (native-born higher than foreign-born, with part of the gap explained by socio-demographics). It further links higher numeracy proficiency to better labour-force participation and lower unemployment risk, and to higher life satisfaction and health, while describing qualification/skills mismatches in employment. Methodological details on PV handling, missing-data treatment, and exact weighting variables are not provided in the excerpt, so uncertainty should be interpreted using the reported confidence intervals rather than inferred from model-based ML performance.
